what_its_for: Ceftazidime is an antibiotic used to fight bacterial infections in your body. It can treat serious infections in your lungs, urinary tract, skin, blood, bones, joints, and brain (meningitis). It works by killing the bacteria that are making you sick. It does NOT work for viral infections like the cold or flu.
how_to_take: Ceftazidime is given as a shot into a vein (IV) or into a muscle (injection). A healthcare professional, nurse, or home health aide will give you this medication. It is usually given in a hospital, clinic, or infusion center, but sometimes it can be given at home with proper training. Never try to give yourself this medication unless your healthcare team has fully trained you and instructed you to do so. Each dose is usually given slowly over 15 to 30 minutes when given into a vein. Make sure to complete the full course of treatment even if you start feeling better, so the infection is fully cleared.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your type of infection, how serious it is, your weight, and how well your kidneys are working. Adults are commonly given 1 to 2 grams every 8 to 12 hours. Children receive doses based on their weight. People with kidney problems may need a lower dose or less frequent dosing. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Since this medication is given by a healthcare professional or on a scheduled home infusion plan, contact your doctor, nurse, or home infusion pharmacy right away if you miss a dose or if a dose is skipped. Do not try to double up or give two doses at once to make up for a missed one. Try to stay on your scheduled dosing times as closely as possible.
storage: If you are receiving ceftazidime at home, store unused vials in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C) in a dry place away from light. Do not freeze the mixed (prepared) solution unless your pharmacist tells you it is safe to do so. Once a vial is mixed, follow your pharmacist's specific instructions on how long you can keep it and at what temperature. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of used needles, syringes, and IV supplies safely in a puncture-proof sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medications, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting ceftazidime. Avoid taking other antibiotics unless your doctor prescribes them. Do not drink alcohol during your treatment, as it may increase the risk of side effects. Avoid driving or using heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or confused. Do not skip doses or stop treatment early without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody, which could be a sign of a serious intestinal infection called C. difficile; seizures or unusual tremors; signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination or swelling in your legs or feet; unusual bruising or bleeding; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); or severe pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site. Also call your doctor if your symptoms are not improving after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: Ceftazidime starts working against bacteria as soon as it enters your body. However, you may not feel better right away. Most people begin to notice improvement within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. It is very important to finish the entire course of antibiotics your doctor prescribed, even if you feel completely better before it is done. Stopping too early can allow the bacteria to come back and become harder to treat.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If your kidneys do not work well, your doctor will lower your dose to prevent the medication from building up to harmful levels in your body. Regular blood tests may be done to monitor your kidney function. Elderly patients: Older adults may have reduced kidney function, so dosing adjustments may be needed. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Ceftazidime may be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, but discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Small amounts of the drug can pass into breast milk. Children: Dosing is based on the child's weight and age. Newborns and premature babies require special dosing and close monitoring.
